mars-and-beyond: Nobody has been to Mars, and a private settlement within 25 years would need a transport system able to carry many people, which does not yet exist. Distance would help once people arrived, because no navy could reach them in less than months. The settlers would still launch under a licence from a state, and Articles VI and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty keep that state responsible for them and in legal control of what it registers. A 2020 clause in Starlink's terms calling Mars a free planet has never been tested, and it is a private contract that binds no government.
asteroids: No one has lived on an asteroid, so the chance of building there is very low. The two companies set up to mine them, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, ran short of money and were sold in 2018 and 2019. Laws in the United States, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and Japan let companies own what they extract. None of those laws gives anyone ownership of the asteroid itself.
moon: Article II of the Outer Space Treaty bans any national claim to the Moon, so there is no legal way to gain title to its land. Countries that signed the Artemis Accords, a non-binding US-led set of principles, treat safety zones around their work as allowed, so whoever arrives first with a state's support has practical influence over a site. The licensing state stays responsible for anyone it sends. Deeds sold to the public since 1980 have no legal effect.
lagrange-cislunar: Lagrange points are places in the Earth-Moon system where gravity holds an object steady. The law there is the same as in low orbit, and supplies would be harder to bring. The L5 Society promoted Gerard O'Neill's colonies at these points in the 1970s and 1980s, and no private habitat has been built.
geo: Geostationary orbit is the ring above the equator where a satellite stays over one spot. Slots and radio frequencies there are handled by the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency, and only its member countries can apply. A habitat would also sit in a crowded band with no way to obtain its own slot. Tonga's filings show that a small country can rent slots to others, and a private group still needs a country to apply for it.
leo: Getting people to low orbit for long stays is plausible because private stations are being built, although none has flown yet. Every object must be on a state's register, and that state keeps legal control over the object and the people on it. Rules agreed among residents and private tokens could work inside that system, but they would give no independence. The $900,000 penalty paid by the company Swarm shows that radio licensing reaches satellites even when they are launched from another country.
stratosphere-near-space: The stratosphere is the layer of air at about 20 kilometres, far above normal air traffic, and no platform there carries people for long stays. No treaty says where a country's airspace ends, so a craft over land may count as being in that country's airspace. In February 2023 US fighters shot down a Chinese balloon at about 60,000 feet off South Carolina, and that shows how a state may respond.
airspace-over-high-seas: No state owns the air above the open ocean, which is why the legal score is higher than over land. Any aircraft still needs a state's registration, and the Tokyo Convention gives that state power over crimes on board. Fuel and maintenance force landings in a country. Some states also require aircraft to identify themselves well outside their own airspace, in areas called air defense identification zones.
airspace-over-states: Article 1 of the Chicago Convention, the main treaty on civil flying, gives each country complete and exclusive sovereignty over the air above its land and territorial waters. A craft can be built and flown there with that country's permission, and the same country can order it down. That leaves no legal basis for self-rule in this air.
ships-flag: Living at sea on a registered ship already works, so the chance of building and staying is high. The World, a ship owned by its residents, has run as a private community since 2002. Villa Vie, a cheaper residential ship, ended in October 2026 when its company could not secure fuel. A ship stays legal by registering with a flag state, whose law applies on board, so residents give up independence to get this stability. A ship with no flag falls under the rules for the high seas.
high-seas: The high seas are the ocean beyond any state's coastal zones. Nobody owns them, so no coastal state holds title, and that gives this place a better legal position than most. Article 89 of the Law of the Sea treaty also bars anyone from claiming them, and Article 110 allows a stateless vessel to be boarded. Open-ocean platforms cost from about $50 million for a small one up to billions, and a wave broke the Aisland barge in two off Dubai in 2024.
central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard: The middle of the Arctic Ocean is high seas, with moving ice and no local supplies, so building there is very hard. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty lets foreigners live and trade on those islands, but under Norway's sovereignty. After a killing on T-3, a drifting ice island, an American court tried the case, and an appeals court split evenly on whether American law applied there.
eez-shelf: The exclusive economic zone is the belt up to 200 nautical miles from a coast where the coastal state controls resources. Article 60 of the Law of the Sea treaty gives that state the exclusive right to authorise artificial islands there, so building one without permission has little legal basis. In 2019 the Thai navy raided a floating home off Phuket that its owners said was just over 12 miles out. Thailand charged the occupants under a law that carries life in prison or death.
territorial-sea: The territorial sea is the belt of water up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, and the coastal state has full sovereignty there. Building is physically easy, but only with that state's permission, so any project becomes a zone granted by a host. Rose Island stood just outside Italian waters as they were then measured, and it was seized about eight weeks after declaring independence. A project inside the limit has even less chance of holding out.
reefs-low-tide-elevations: Reefs that are under water at high tide cannot be claimed by occupying them, according to the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling, and piling up sand does not change that. Founders tried the Minerva Reefs, Silver Shoals and the Misteriosa Bank. Nearby states responded by annexing the reef, sending gunboats or suing, or the plan collapsed as a fraud case. A reef therefore offers a physical base with little legal protection.
abandoned-platforms: Sealand has lasted since 1967 because its fort stood outside Britain's three-mile limit at the time, and Britain has left it alone since the limit grew to 12 miles in 1987. A new project would not have that history. On a continental shelf or in an exclusive economic zone, the coastal state has legal power over installations, and disused ones must be removed for shipping safety. Buying a platform transfers ownership of the structure only.
disputed-islands: Islands such as the Spratlys and Paracels in the South China Sea are held by garrisons of several states, so a private claimant would be among rival navies. In 1956 the Filipino businessman Tomás Cloma claimed part of the Spratlys as Freedomland. Taiwan later burned buildings there, and in 1974 the Philippines arrested him and made him sign over his rights. States with existing claims have little reason to accept a new one.
undersea-water-column: Undersea habitats such as Aquarius off Florida exist as permitted research stations, so building one is possible. The water follows the rules of the surface zone above it, and the seabed belongs either to a coastal state's shelf or to the international system. Going deeper therefore brings no new legal shelter. Staying long term also depends on supply from the surface.
deep-seabed-area: The deep seabed outside every country's control is called the Area. Article 137 of the Law of the Sea treaty bars any claim to it, and only the International Seabed Authority can issue mining contracts, to operators backed by a member country. The authority's mining rules are still unfinished. Deepsea Ventures, an American company, made a private claim to part of it in 1974, and no report says it led to any mining or court ruling.
terra-nullius-land: Terra nullius means land that belongs to no state, and some exists. States do not treat it as open to private founders, since international law lets only states acquire it. Bir Tawil, between Egypt and Sudan, has no water source and can be reached only through those countries. Croatia polices Gornja Siga on the Danube and arrests people who settle there. Older places of this kind, such as Moresnet and Cospaia, lasted only while their neighbours agreed.
antarctica-unclaimed: Marie Byrd Land is the one large part of Antarctica no country claims, but Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty bars any new claim. The Madrid Protocol, an environmental add-on to the treaty, bans mining. No claimant has built anything there, and Westarctica, Flandrensis and Talossa exist only on paper. The area is also among the hardest places on Earth to reach, and most routes pass through a treaty member's territory.
antarctica-claimed: Seven states hold claims here that the Antarctic Treaty has frozen, and treaty members must give notice of expeditions from their territory, so access is hard to arrange independently. Greenpeace ran the only non-government year-round base, World Park Base, from 1987 until 1991 as a campaign and then removed it. Chile and Argentina have placed families and recorded births in the region, and the treaty says even those acts cannot support a claim. A private group would have much less standing than either of them.
inside-state: Declaring a micronation on land inside a country is easy, and many such claims last for years when the state finds them harmless. Hutt River in Australia ran for 50 years, and its owners were still ordered to pay millions in tax. The country's law keeps applying whatever passports or titles the founder issues. Recognition is very unlikely, because no state has any reason to accept a part of another state on the strength of a declaration.
host-state-carve-outs: This is the most workable route to separate courts and tax rules, because the host government grants them by its own law. The Dubai International Financial Centre has had its own common-law courts, based on past rulings in the English style, since 2006. A later government can reverse the grant. Honduras's Supreme Court struck down its special zones in 2024, and the Próspera zone now relies on an investment claim against the state. The zone remains part of the host country, so this route does not produce recognition as a separate state.
unrecognised-state: Places such as Somaliland, Transnistria and Northern Cyprus run real governments on land another state claims, usually after war or with the help of a supporting state's army. A private group cannot start one, so the chance of building is low, while the governments that exist hold their land fairly well. Israel's recognition of Somaliland in December 2025 is a rare recent gain, after 34 years of self-rule. Artsakh shows the risk, since Azerbaijan ended it by force in 2023.
digital-no-territory: Anyone can found an online nation, and there is no place for a government to raid, so starting and continuing are easy. It holds no land, and every member and server stays under the law of the place where it sits. Bitnation faded out, and the Network School lost its Malaysian business licence in July 2026. The Order of Malta keeps diplomatic relations with no territory, but its standing comes from centuries of history that a new group cannot copy.
interstellar-ships: No crewed ship able to reach another star exists or has funding, and Project Hyperion and the 100 Year Starship are only studies. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty sets no distance at which the registering state's legal control ends, although a ship years from Earth could not be reached in practice. The high figure for holding on reflects that distance alone.
the-sun: No one can go to the Sun, so every figure is zero. The best-known claim is that of María Ángeles Durán of Spain, who had a notary record her statement of ownership in 2010 and sold plots on eBay until eBay removed the listings. A notary's record shows that a person made a statement, and it gives no sovereignty.
outer-moons: Titan, Europa, Callisto and Ceres exist in plans only as paper studies, such as NASA's 2003 HOPE study of Callisto and Pekka Janhunen's design for a settlement orbiting Ceres. Travel would take years, which would keep other states away and also make rescue impossible. The Outer Space Treaty's ban on claiming land in space covers these bodies too. That combination gives a very low chance of building and a fairly high chance of holding on once there.
venus-clouds: The conditions about 55 kilometres above Venus are mild, about 27 C at half of Earth's air pressure, which is why NASA's HAVOC study chose that height. It was a paper study that received no further funding, and nothing has flown. In law Venus is treated like the Moon, so no one can claim it.
orbital-megastructures: Large space colonies have been designed since the 1975 Stanford torus and have never been funded, so the chance of building one is very low. The law is the same as for an ordinary space station, which means a state must register and oversee it. A space elevator, a cable running from the ground into space, would also rest on the ground or sea at one end, within a state's reach.
airborne-habitats: Nobody lives permanently in the air. Sky Cruise is an animation, and Stratobus is an uncrewed airship still at the test-model stage. Any aircraft needs a state's registration and somewhere to land or receive supplies, and the air over a country belongs to that country. These needs keep the legal and holding chances low.
new-land: New islands almost always rise in some country's waters, so a state can claim them at once. In 1831 the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and Britain both claimed Graham Island within weeks, and it wore away within months. Volcanic islands can also vanish, as the 2015 island at Hunga Tonga mostly did in the 2022 eruption. So new land gives a founder neither a legal opening nor a reliable base.
inland-waters: Lakes and rivers lie between or inside countries, so every island has at least one state close by. Kenya and Uganda have clashed over Migingo, a rock of about 2,000 square metres in Lake Victoria, and Ugandan officials were still seizing Kenyan fishermen's gear in 2025. On Lake Constance no treaty sets the border in the deep water, but each country's view gives the water to one or more of the shore states. Building is easy, and it would happen under an existing country's control.
floating-ice: Writers disagree about what a free-floating iceberg is in law, and no court has settled it, so the legal position is uncertain. Icebergs also melt. A23a, once the world's largest at about 3,500 square kilometres, was gone or nearly gone by July 2026. Soviet and Russian drifting stations show that people can live on sea ice with a state's support. A private group would have to manage that without one.
underground-subseabed: Digging is easy, which is why the chance of building is high. Land ownership and a coastal state's control of its shelf both run downward, so existing law applies below the surface. CyberBunker, in former NATO bunkers in the Netherlands and Germany, called itself a republic. German police raided its second bunker in 2019, and a court convicted all eight defendants of belonging to a criminal organisation.
buy-from-a-state: The founders of Minerva and Operation Atlantis and the Russian businessman Anton Bakov looked for a government willing to sell and found none, and no private purchase in the 20th or 21st century is known to have produced sovereignty. Private buyers did get ruling rights in earlier centuries, when an emperor, sultan or king agreed. Liechtenstein became sovereign in 1806 after purchases around 1700, and the Brookes in Sarawak and the North Borneo Company ruled under grants made in the 1800s until 1946. Buying land today, as Kiribati did in Fiji for $8.6 million, leaves the seller's law in force. If a state did give up land by treaty to a new government, the title would be strong, which explains the high legal and holding figures.
leases-and-extraterritorial-spots: Guantánamo Bay shows a lease lasting since 1903, at $4,085 a year, but it is between two states. Private groups have no comparable deal, and the closest is the Order of Malta's treaty rights at Fort St Angelo in Malta, where Malta keeps ownership. Embassies and airports have sheltered people for years, including Julian Assange and Mehran Karimi Nasseri. No territory passed to any of them.
run-by-international-agreement: Danzig, Tangier and Trieste were set up by powerful states that were ending wars or settling rivalries, and each ended when those states changed course. A private founder has no way to start this process, so the chance of building is very low. Such places have some legal standing while they last because they rest on treaties, and that explains the middle figures for law and holding.
buffer-zones: Buffer zones are strips of land kept between opposing forces. People do live in some of them, including about 10,000 in Cyprus's UN buffer zone and two villages in the Korean demilitarised zone. They live under peacekeepers or military authorities, which leaves no room for a new government. Chernobyl's self-settlers are mostly elderly people whom local officials unofficially let stay. None of these places offers a legal basis for self-rule.
secession-and-decolonisation: This is the route that has actually produced new states, and it needs an existing people and territory, so a private founder scores low. For a real population the odds are far better. Wikipedia's table lists about 123 independence votes since 1817, and 31 of them led to independence and recognition. South Sudan and Montenegro had a peace deal or constitutional right behind their votes, and Eritrea had won its war. Catalonia and Biafra had none of these and did not succeed.
taking-over-a-state-or-town: Moving voters into a town can work for a while, under the existing state's law. Followers of Rajneesh outvoted the residents of Antelope, Oregon, in 1982, and supporters of the Free State Project held 17 of 400 seats in New Hampshire's House in 2017 to 2018. Mercenary coups have mostly failed, in the Seychelles in 1981 and Equatorial Guinea in 2004, and the plotters were arrested. Bob Denard's long control of the Comoros is the exception, and it ended too.
indigenous-prior-sovereignty: These figures apply to peoples with an existing claim, which a new founder cannot acquire. Gains have come through negotiation and court rulings, such as the creation of Nunavut in 1999 and the McGirt decision in 2020. Haudenosaunee passports have been accepted by some states and refused by others, including Britain in 2010. These routes expand self-rule inside the existing state, which explains the low figure for recognition.
exile-and-landless-authority: A government in exile holds no land, so there is little for a state to seize once a host allows it to operate. The Central Tibetan Administration has run elections and services from India since 1959. It depends on India's tolerance, and no country recognises it as a sovereign government.
no-territory-conceptual: Anyone can declare a country that exists only as an idea, and many people have, including John Lennon and Yoko Ono with Nutopia in 1973. Nothing can be raided, because nothing is held. Members remain under the ordinary law of wherever they live, and that keeps the legal and recognition figures low.
